title: Electromagnetic Spectrum: Production and Uses of EM Waves

claims.text: Overview of the electromagnetic spectrum, ordered by wavelength: starting from the visible range (roughly 400 nm to 700 nm), UV lies to the shorter-wavelength side (10 nm to 400 nm), followed by X-rays (1 angstrom to 100 angstrom) and gamma rays (10^-3 angstrom to 1 angstrom) at even shorter wavelengths -- gamma rays obtained from nuclear reactions. On the longer-wavelength side of visible: infrared (700 nm to 1 mm), then microwaves (1 mm to 0.3 m), then radio waves (0.3 m to 10^5 m). Moving from visible towards shorter wavelengths, wavelength decreases (frequency increases); moving towards longer wavelengths, wavelength increases (frequency decreases). There is no sharp demarcation between adjacent bands -- they overlap at the boundaries, and different sources may cite slightly different boundary values (e.g. 700 nm vs 720 nm for red). A common exam question asks to arrange given radiation types in ascending/descending order of frequency using this ordering

Radio waves: produced by accelerated motion of charges in a conducting wire. Used in radio and television communication systems. AM radio band: 500 kHz to 1710 kHz. TV waves: around 54 MHz to 890 MHz. FM radio band: 88 MHz to 108 MHz (station frequencies like 92.7 MHz, 98.3 MHz lie in this range). Mobile phone frequencies are higher still, known as ultra-high frequencies

Microwaves: wavelength range roughly 0.1 m to 1 mm -- essentially the short-wavelength end of the radio wave region (sometimes classified as part of it, but distinguished by their much shorter wavelength). Produced by special vacuum tubes called klystrons or magnetrons. Used in RADAR systems (radio detection and ranging) -- their short wavelength gives high energy and good directional properties (not easily diffracted by objects, travel in straight lines), which is why radar antennas can transmit a narrow beam and detect reflections from objects precisely. Also used in microwave ovens: the microwave frequency is chosen to match the resonant frequency of water molecules, so energy transfers efficiently into the molecules' kinetic energy (via matching the frequency of their own oscillation about their mean position), raising the temperature of food containing water

Infrared: wavelength range 1 mm to 700 nm. Produced by hot bodies and molecules. Also called 'heat waves', because water molecules present in most materials readily absorb infrared radiation, increasing their thermal motion and heating up their surroundings (this is why you feel warmth standing near a fire). Uses: infrared lamps in physiotherapy; electronic devices such as remote controls and remote switches

Greenhouse effect (explained via infrared absorption): using the analogy of a closed car heating up in sunlight -- high-energy UV rays from the sun enter through the glass; after striking the interior, their energy is reduced (re-emitted as lower-energy infrared), and this infrared can no longer easily escape back out through the glass, so the trapped energy raises the interior temperature. Similarly for Earth: incoming solar radiation is absorbed and partly re-radiated as infrared, which is then trapped by greenhouse gases (e.g. methane, water vapour, carbon dioxide) in the atmosphere rather than escaping to space -- keeping the Earth's surface warmer than it would otherwise be, including maintaining warmth overnight

Visible light: wavelength range roughly 700 nm to 400 nm. Produced by lamps and ionized gases. Its primary use/importance: visible light emitted or reflected from objects around us provides information about the world -- it is how we see. Also used to study molecular structure and the arrangement of electrons in the outer shells of atoms

Ultraviolet (UV) rays: wavelength range roughly 400 nm to 0.6 nm. Produced by special lamps and very hot bodies (the Sun being the primary natural source). Uses: focused into narrow beams for high-precision applications such as LASIK eye surgery (a commonly asked board-exam question); UV lamps used in water purification systems to kill germs; used to detect forged documents and fingerprints. Caution: depletion of the ozone layer by chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) is a matter of concern, since the ozone layer normally filters out harmful UV radiation from reaching the Earth's surface

X-rays: produced by bombardment of high-energy electrons onto a heavy metal target (inside a Coolidge tube -- a large potential difference accelerates the electrons before they strike the metal). Used as a diagnostic tool in medicine (X-ray imaging), in the treatment of certain forms of cancer, and in scientific research to reveal the structure of molecules (X-ray crystallography). Because X-rays are high-frequency/high-energy and can harm healthy cells with prolonged exposure, medical/diagnostic exposure to X-rays is kept to a very short duration, not prolonged

Gamma rays: wavelength less than 10^-3 nm -- the highest-frequency, highest-energy radiations in the EM spectrum. Produced in nuclear reactions and emitted by radioactive nuclei. Uses: in medicine, to destroy cancer cells; used for the study of atomic nuclei; and, because of their very high energy, gamma rays are also used to produce (induce) nuclear reactions

markdown_body:
## The electromagnetic spectrum (NCERT 8.5)

Ordered by wavelength around the visible range ($\approx400$–$700$ nm):

| Band | Wavelength range |
|---|---|
| Radio waves | $0.3$ m – $10^5$ m |
| Microwaves | $1$ mm – $0.3$ m |
| Infrared | $700$ nm – $1$ mm |
| **Visible** | $400$ nm – $700$ nm |
| UV | $10$ nm – $400$ nm |
| X-rays | $1$ Å – $100$ Å |
| Gamma rays | $10^{-3}$ Å – $1$ Å |

No sharp boundaries — adjacent bands overlap, and cited boundary values vary slightly by source. Moving from visible toward shorter wavelength, frequency increases; toward longer wavelength, frequency decreases. (Common exam question: arrange given radiation types in ascending/descending order of frequency.)

### Production and uses, band by band

**Radio waves** — produced by accelerated charges in a conducting wire. Radio/TV communication: AM band $500$–$1710$ kHz, TV $\approx54$–$890$ MHz, FM band $88$–$108$ MHz; mobile phones use even higher (ultra-high) frequencies.

**Microwaves** — produced by klystrons/magnetrons. Used in **radar** (short wavelength $\Rightarrow$ high energy, good directionality, minimal diffraction, straight-line travel) and **microwave ovens** (frequency tuned to water molecules' resonant frequency for efficient energy transfer, heating food).

**Infrared** — produced by hot bodies/molecules; also called *heat waves* (water molecules readily absorb IR, raising thermal motion). Used in physiotherapy lamps, remote controls. Also explains the **greenhouse effect**: incoming solar UV/energy is absorbed and re-radiated as IR, which greenhouse gases (CH$_4$, H$_2$O, CO$_2$) trap in the atmosphere, warming the surface (analogous to a closed car heating in sunlight).

**Visible light** — produced by lamps, ionized gases. Lets us see objects (light emitted/reflected carries information about the world); also used to study molecular structure and electron arrangement.

**UV rays** — produced by special lamps and very hot bodies (the Sun). Used in LASIK eye surgery, water purification (killing germs), detecting forged documents/fingerprints. **Caution:** ozone-layer depletion by CFCs is a concern, since ozone normally filters harmful UV.

**X-rays** — produced by high-energy electrons bombarding a heavy metal target (Coolidge tube). Used diagnostically in medicine, in cancer treatment, and in scientific research (revealing molecular structure) — exposure kept brief since prolonged exposure harms healthy cells.

**Gamma rays** — wavelength $<10^{-3}$ nm, the highest-energy band; produced in nuclear reactions/emitted by radioactive nuclei. Used in medicine to destroy cancer cells, to study atomic nuclei, and (due to their high energy) to induce nuclear reactions.
